items.q: (A) No sooner the bell had rung than the students, (B) most of whom had been dreading the test, (C) poured out of the hall (D) as if released from a cage.
options: No sooner the bell had rung
most of whom had been dreading
as if released from a cage
items.correction: No sooner had the bell rung
items.explanation: A fronted negative adverbial such as No sooner forces subject–auxiliary inversion: No sooner had the bell rung than…

items.q: The board of governors (A) insisted that the headmaster (B) resigns immediately, (C) citing the unexplained disappearance of funds (D) earmarked for the new library.
items.explanation: After verbs of demand such as insist, demand, suggest, recommend, the that-clause takes the present subjunctive (base form): that the headmaster resign.

items.q: Having been delayed by fog for six hours, (A) the airline offered the exhausted passengers meal vouchers, (B) which few of them (C) bothered to use, (D) most preferring to doze on the floor.
options: the airline offered the exhausted passengers meal vouchers
most preferring to doze on the floor
items.correction: the exhausted passengers were offered meal vouchers by the airline
items.explanation: A participle clause describes the subject of the main clause, and it was the passengers, not the airline, who had been delayed; as written the opening clause is a dangling modifier, so the passengers must become the subject: the exhausted passengers were offered meal vouchers by the airline.

items.q: The team, (A) whose radio failed on the second day, (B) would not be stranded on the glacier now (C) if they packed enough fuel (D) before setting out.
options: would not be stranded on the glacier now
items.correction: if they had packed enough fuel
items.explanation: A mixed conditional: a past condition (packing fuel) with a present result (now) needs the past perfect in the if-clause, if they had packed.

items.q: The new evidence (A) unearthed at the site (B) has led several historians (C) to question the accepted date and (D) to make doubt on the temple's origin.
items.explanation: The fixed collocation is cast doubt on something; make doubt is not an English verb–noun pairing.

items.q: (A) A great number of research into sleep (B) suggests that teenagers (C) who go to bed after midnight (D) perform markedly worse in memory tasks.
options: who go to bed after midnight
items.explanation: Research is uncountable, so it takes a great deal of / a lot of; a great number of is only used with plural countable nouns.

items.q: The coach (A) now bitterly wishes that he (B) has substituted his exhausted striker before the final ten minutes, (C) during which the opposing team (D) scored twice.
items.explanation: A wish about the past is expressed with the past perfect: wishes that he had substituted; the present perfect cannot follow wish.

items.q: (A) It was the ash cloud what grounded thousands of flights, (B) rather than the lava itself, (C) which never travelled (D) more than a few kilometres from the crater.
options: It was the ash cloud what grounded
items.correction: It was the ash cloud that grounded
items.explanation: In an it-cleft sentence the focused element is followed by that (or who/which), never by what, which cannot introduce a relative clause after a noun.

items.q: Successful applicants must demonstrate (A) an ability to work independently, (B) a willingness to take criticism and (C) that they communicate clearly, (D) both in writing and in speech.
options: both in writing and in speech
items.explanation: Items in a list must be parallel: two noun phrases (an ability…, a willingness…) cannot be followed by a that-clause, so the third item needs the same noun-phrase form.

items.q: Not until the reservoirs (A) had fallen to a fifth of capacity (B) did the authorities admit the severity of the crisis, (C) and under no circumstances (D) they would consider rationing.
options: had fallen to a fifth of capacity
items.explanation: When a negative adverbial such as under no circumstances opens a clause, the auxiliary must come before the subject: would they consider.

items.q: The union (A) has demanded that every worker (B) exposed to the chemical (C) is tested by an independent doctor (D) at the company's expense.
options: is tested by an independent doctor
items.correction: be tested by an independent doctor
items.explanation: Demand that introduces a clause in the subjunctive, so the verb keeps its base form regardless of the subject: that every worker be tested.

items.q: (A) Written in a hurry, the editor rejected the article, (B) arguing that (C) its central claim (D) rested on a single unverified source.
options: rested on a single unverified source
items.correction: Because it had been written in a hurry
items.explanation: The participle Written in a hurry grammatically describes the nearest subject, the editor, which is absurd: a dangling participle must be replaced by a clause with its own subject.

items.q: (A) Having examined only three samples, the researchers (B) took the conclusion that the river was safe, (C) a claim their own supervisor (D) later dismissed as premature.
items.explanation: The collocation is draw / reach / come to a conclusion; take a conclusion is not used in English.

items.q: Her (A) insistence on punctuality, (B) combined with an almost obsessive (C) attention to detail, made her (D) ideally suited of the job.
items.explanation: The adjective suited is followed by to (or for) a role: suited to the job; of is not possible here.

items.q: Neither the captain (A) nor the two engineers (B) who inspected the hull (C) was aware that the crack had (D) widened overnight.
items.explanation: With neither … nor the verb agrees with the nearer subject; the two engineers is plural, so the verb must be were.

items.q: The council (A) has pledged to plant twice (B) as many trees as it (C) removed last year, though critics say (D) the amount of saplings ordered is far too small.
items.explanation: Saplings is a plural countable noun, so it takes the number of; the amount of is reserved for uncountable nouns.

items.q: (A) If the river would not have burst its banks, the harvest (B) might have been saved and the villagers (C) would not now be dependent on (D) food parcels.
options: If the river would not have burst its banks
would not now be dependent on
items.correction: If the river had not burst its banks
items.explanation: Would never appears in the if-clause of an unreal conditional; a past condition takes the past perfect, if the river had not burst, and the result clauses may then be past or present.

items.q: (A) Only after the second explosion (B) the miners realised that the tunnel behind them (C) had collapsed, cutting off (D) their only route to the surface.
options: their only route to the surface
items.explanation: A fronted Only after / Only when phrase triggers inversion in the main clause: Only after the second explosion did the miners realise.

items.q: The examiner asked the candidates (A) why they had chosen the topic (B) and whether (C) could they summarise it in a sentence, (D) which few managed to do.
options: why they had chosen the topic
could they summarise it in a sentence
items.correction: they could summarise it in a sentence
items.explanation: In a reported question the subject comes before the verb, as in a statement: whether they could summarise, not the direct-question order could they.

items.q: The two chess prodigies, (A) both of whom learned the game before (B) they could read, now spend every evening (C) analysing openings (D) with each another.
items.explanation: The reciprocal pronouns are each other and one another; each another mixes the two and does not exist.

items.q: (A) The most sophisticated a piece of software becomes, (B) the greater the temptation (C) to accept its conclusions (D) without asking how they were reached.
options: The most sophisticated a piece of software becomes
without asking how they were reached
items.correction: The more sophisticated a piece of software becomes
items.explanation: A double comparative (the … the …) needs comparative forms in both halves: The more sophisticated …, the greater …; a superlative cannot fill the first slot.

items.q: The (A) rapid expansion of the city's suburbs has placed (B) a considerably strain on the water supply, (C) which was designed for (D) barely half the current population.
items.explanation: A noun (strain) is modified by an adjective, considerable; the adverb considerably can only modify a verb, adjective or another adverb.

items.q: (A) Little is known about the composer's early years, (B) except that he was raised by an aunt (C) who played the violin in orchestra (D) of a provincial theatre.
options: except that he was raised by an aunt
who played the violin in orchestra
items.correction: who played the violin in the orchestra
items.explanation: Orchestra is a singular countable noun made definite by the following of-phrase, so it needs the: in the orchestra of a provincial theatre.

items.q: The team (A) pressed on towards the summit (B) despite two members (C) showing early signs of altitude sickness, (D) even the guides had warned them the night before.
options: showing early signs of altitude sickness
even the guides had warned them
items.correction: even though the guides had warned them
items.explanation: Even is an adverb and cannot join two clauses; the concessive conjunction is even though (or although).

items.q: (A) Not wanted to appear ungrateful, the guest (B) forced down a second helping of the stew, (C) which tasted (D) as though it had been boiled for a week.
options: as though it had been boiled
items.explanation: The guest is the one doing the wanting, so the participle clause must be active, with the -ing form: Not wanting to appear; the past participle would make the guest the object of the wanting.

items.q: (A) What worries the marine biologists most (B) are the speed at which the coral (C) has lost its colour, (D) rather than the loss itself.
options: What worries the marine biologists most
items.explanation: In a wh-cleft the what-clause is a singular subject, and its complement here (the speed) is also singular, so the linking verb must be is.

items.q: (A) In the wake of the scandal, the newspaper's circulation (B) fell so sharply that (C) it was in the verge of closure (D) within eighteen months.
options: In the wake of the scandal
it was in the verge of closure
items.correction: it was on the verge of closure
items.explanation: The idiom is on the verge of (doing / something); a verge is an edge, and one stands on an edge, not in it.

items.q: The volunteers (A) had been rebuilding the school for barely a week (B) when the second earthquake struck, (C) undoing everything (D) they achieved so far.
items.explanation: So far measures progress up to a reference point; from the past viewpoint of the earthquake that requires the past perfect, everything they had achieved so far.

items.q: The mountain village (A) where we spent the summer, (B) most of them houses date from the eighteenth century, (C) has no road (D) wide enough for a car.
options: most of them houses date from
items.correction: most of whose houses date from
items.explanation: A non-defining clause expressing possession is built with quantifier + of + whose: most of whose houses; them leaves the clause with no relative link to the village.

items.q: (A) Far from putting off by the criticism, the young director (B) went on to make (C) a second film that (D) silenced even her harshest reviewers.
options: Far from putting off by the criticism
items.correction: Far from being put off by the criticism
items.explanation: The director was the one affected by the criticism, so the phrasal verb needs a passive -ing form after the preposition: far from being put off by.
